evidence.reference_title: Clinical and genetic spectrum of AMPD2-related pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 9.
evidence.snippet: We identified homozygous or compound heterozygous AMPD2 variants in eight PCH-affected individuals from six families.

evidence.reference_title: Clinical and genetic spectrum of AMPD2-related pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 9.
evidence.snippet: The existence of various AMPD2 isoforms with different functions possibly explains the variability in phenotypes associated with AMPD2 variants: variants leaving some of the isoforms intact may cause SPG63, while those affecting all isoforms may result in the severe and early-onset PCH9.

nodes.description: In PCH1A, biallelic VRK1 loss-of-function mutations impair nuclear envelope formation and RNA processing in post-mitotic neurons. Motor neurons of the anterior horn of the spinal cord are additionally affected beyond pontocerebellar neurons, producing a spinal muscular atrophy-like clinical picture (hypotonia, muscle weakness, areflexia) superimposed on pontocerebellar hypoplasia.

evidence.reference_title: Spinal muscular atrophy with pontocerebellar hypoplasia is caused by a mutation in the VRK1 gene.

evidence.reference_title: Spinal muscular atrophy with pontocerebellar hypoplasia is caused by a mutation in the VRK1 gene.
evidence.snippet: VRK1, one of three members of the mammalian VRK family, is a serine/threonine kinase that phosphorylates p53 and CREB and is essential for nuclear envelope formation.

evidence.reference_title: CHMP1A encodes an essential regulator of BMI1-INK4A in cerebellar development.
evidence.snippet: Here, we show that loss-of-function mutations in human CHMP1A cause reduced cerebellar size (pontocerebellar hypoplasia) and reduced cerebral cortical size (microcephaly).

evidence.reference_title: Human CLP1 mutations alter tRNA biogenesis, affecting both peripheral and central nervous system function.
evidence.snippet: Thus, we have identified a defined clinical syndrome with progressive central and peripheral nervous system defects in 11 affected children from five families, all of whom carry a homozygous CLP1 R140H mutation.

evidence.reference_title: COASY related pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 12: A common Indian mutation with expansion of the phenotypic spectrum.
evidence.snippet: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia (PCH) type 12 is a rare, perinatal lethal neurodegenerative genetic disorder caused by biallelic mutations in the COASY gene.

evidence.reference_title: CoA synthase plays a critical role in neurodevelopment and neurodegeneration.
evidence.snippet: Recessive variants of this gene cause an exceptionally rare and devastating disease called COASY protein-associated neurodegeneration (CoPAN) while complete loss-of-function variants in COASY have been identified in fetuses/neonates with Pontocerebellar Hypoplasia type 12 (PCH 12).

nodes.description: PRDM13 is a transcriptional repressor expressed in progenitors of the cerebellar ventricular zone, which give rise to the cerebellar GABAergic neurons including Purkinje cells. Biallelic PRDM13 loss produces a PCH-like phenotype with hypoplasia of the inferior olive, dysplasia of the dentate nucleus, and a sparse, disorganised Purkinje cell layer, so the lesion here is a failure of neuronal specification rather than of a housekeeping process.

evidence.reference_title: Recessive PRDM13 mutations cause fatal perinatal brainstem dysfunction with cerebellar hypoplasia and disrupt Purkinje cell differentiation.
evidence.snippet: We describe four families with children presenting with severe neonatal brainstem dysfunction and pronounced deficits in cognitive and motor development associated with four different bi-allelic mutations in PRDM13, including homozygous truncating variants in the most severely affected individuals.

evidence.reference_title: Recessive PRDM13 mutations cause fatal perinatal brainstem dysfunction with cerebellar hypoplasia and disrupt Purkinje cell differentiation.
evidence.snippet: Brain MRI and fetopathological examination revealed a PCH-like phenotype, associated with major hypoplasia of inferior olive nuclei and dysplasia of the dentate nucleus.

evidence.reference_title: Recessive PRDM13 mutations cause fatal perinatal brainstem dysfunction with cerebellar hypoplasia and disrupt Purkinje cell differentiation.
evidence.snippet: Notably, histopathological examinations highlighted a sparse and disorganized Purkinje cell layer in the cerebellum.

nodes.description: Hypoplasia of the cerebellum is the cardinal structural finding, present in all PCH types. Prenatal onset with progressive postnatal atrophy. In PCH2, the characteristic "dragonfly" MRI pattern shows flat, severely reduced cerebellar hemispheres with relative sparing of the vermis.

evidence.reference_title: Classification, diagnosis and potential mechanisms in pontocerebellar hypoplasia.
evidence.snippet: All subtypes share common characteristics, including hypoplasia/atrophy of cerebellum and pons, progressive microcephaly, and variable cerebral involvement.

nodes.description: COASY encodes CoA synthase, which carries out the last steps of de novo coenzyme A biosynthesis. Near-complete loss of function gives the perinatal lethal PCH12 phenotype, whereas hypomorphic COASY alleles cause COASY protein-associated neurodegeneration, a form of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation.

evidence.reference_title: COASY related pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 12: A common Indian mutation with expansion of the phenotypic spectrum.
evidence.snippet: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia (PCH) type 12 is a rare, perinatal lethal neurodegenerative genetic disorder caused by biallelic mutations in the COASY gene.

evidence.reference_title: CoA synthase plays a critical role in neurodevelopment and neurodegeneration.
evidence.snippet: Recessive variants of this gene cause an exceptionally rare and devastating disease called COASY protein-associated neurodegeneration (CoPAN) while complete loss-of-function variants in COASY have been identified in fetuses/neonates with Pontocerebellar Hypoplasia type 12 (PCH 12).

nodes.description: Hyperkinetic movement disorder with chorea and dystonia, characteristic of PCH2. Dyskinesia is associated with TSEN54 mutations and can be a prominent presenting feature in the first months of life.

evidence.reference_title: Clinical, neuroradiological and genetic findings in pontocerebellar hypoplasia.
evidence.snippet: Mutations in TSEN54 are clinically associated with dyskinesia and/or dystonia and variable degrees of spasticity, in some cases with pure generalized spasticity.

nodes.description: CHMP1A is a subunit of the ESCRT-III membrane-remodelling complex. In null mice, loss of Chmp1a impairs intraluminal vesicle formation in multivesicular bodies and Sonic hedgehog secretion, and the cortical and cerebellar progenitors fail to proliferate; in patient cells the proliferation defect tracks increased INK4A expression and loss of its normal BMI1 repression. Biallelic loss of function gives PCH8. The proliferation arm rather than the trafficking arm is what the cited sources tie to reduced cerebellar size, so this node is kept separate from the TBC1D23 Golgi node.

evidence.snippet: In Chmp1a null mice, this defect is associated with impaired sonic hedgehog (Shh) secretion and intraluminal vesicle (ILV) formation in multivesicular bodies (MVBs).

nodes.description: Feeding difficulty is a common severe-care feature in PCH, reflecting profound neurodevelopmental impairment, hypotonia, dysphagia, and respiratory vulnerability. In RARS2-related PCH6 it accompanies progressive microcephaly and virtual absence of psychomotor development.

nodes.description: TBC1D23 is a Golgi-localised adaptor that bridges endosome-derived vesicles to golgins during retrograde transport and is required for LKB1 signalling at the Golgi. Biallelic loss gives PCH11, which has been reported as a non-degenerative PCH subtype with postnatal rather than prenatal cerebellar change, setting it apart from the RNA-processing forms.

evidence.reference_title: TBC1D23 mediates Golgi-specific LKB1 signaling.
evidence.snippet: TBC1D23, a Golgi-localized protein that is frequently mutated in the neurodevelopment disorder pontocerebellar hypoplasia (PCH), is specifically required for the LKB1 signaling at the Golgi.

evidence.reference_title: Identification and functional analysis of a novel TBC1D23 pathogenic variant in a Chinese family with pontocerebellar hypoplasia.
evidence.snippet: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 11 (PCH11) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by variants in TBC1D23.

evidence.reference_title: Homozygous Mutations in TBC1D23 Lead to a Non-degenerative Form of Pontocerebellar Hypoplasia.
evidence.snippet: Here, we report biallelic TBC1D23 mutations in six individuals from four unrelated families manifesting a non-degenerative form of PCH.

evidence.reference_title: TBC1D23 mediates Golgi-specific LKB1 signaling.
evidence.snippet: TBC1D23 was previously identified as a bridging factor for endosome-derived vesicles and golgins at Trans-Golgi Network (TGN)

evidence.reference_title: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 11: Does the genetic defect determine timing of cerebellar pathology?
evidence.snippet: While pontine hypoplasia and pronounced microcephaly are in line with previous reports on PCH11, our observations of clearly postnatal atrophy of the cerebellum argues for a different pathomechanism than in the other forms of PCH and supports the hypothesis that TBC1D23 deficiency predominantly interferes with postnatal rather than with prenatal cerebellar development.

nodes.description: Pontine hypoplasia accompanies cerebellar hypoplasia in most PCH types, reflecting degeneration of pontine nuclei and transverse pontine fibres.

evidence.reference_title: tRNA splicing endonuclease mutations cause pontocerebellar hypoplasia.
evidence.snippet: Pontocerebellar hypoplasias (PCH) represent a group of neurodegenerative autosomal recessive disorders with prenatal onset, atrophy or hypoplasia of the cerebellum, hypoplasia of the ventral pons, microcephaly, variable neocortical atrophy and severe mental and motor impairments.

nodes.description: Neonatal and infantile hypotonia, often severe, contributing to feeding difficulties, respiratory compromise, and absence of motor milestones. In PCH1A, hypotonia is compounded by anterior horn cell degeneration.

evidence.reference_title: Spinal muscular atrophy with pontocerebellar hypoplasia is caused by a mutation in the VRK1 gene.
evidence.snippet: The spinal muscular atrophies (SMAs) are a genetically and clinically heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by degeneration and loss of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord, leading to muscle weakness and atrophy.

nodes.description: Convergent downstream consequence of TSEN complex dysfunction, mitochondrial tRNA synthetase deficiency, and motor neuron degeneration. Pontocerebellar neurons fail to develop normally in utero (prenatal onset), followed by progressive postnatal degeneration. Neuropathology shows reduced cerebellar volume, simplified or absent foliation, and hypoplastic pons with loss of pontine nuclei. The cerebral cortex is relatively spared. MRI shows the characteristic dragonfly or butterfly sign of hypoplastic cerebellar hemispheres with preserved vermis in PCH2.

nodes.description: MINPP1 is a multiple inositol polyphosphate phosphatase. Biallelic loss of function allows the chelator inositol hexakisphosphate to accumulate inside cells, which has been proposed as the route to the PCH16 phenotype.

evidence.reference_title: MINPP1 prevents intracellular accumulation of the chelator inositol hexakisphosphate and is mutated in Pontocerebellar Hypoplasia.
evidence.snippet: These data suggest the involvement of IP6-mediated chelation on Pontocerebellar Hypoplasia disease pathology and thereby highlight the critical role of MINPP1 in the regulation of human brain development and homeostasis.

nodes.description: SLC25A46 encodes a mitochondrial outer-membrane protein that tunes mitochondrial fission and fusion. Complete loss of function gives the lethal congenital PCH1E phenotype, while milder alleles of the same gene cause optic atrophy and hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy, so the severity of the PCH phenotype tracks the severity of the allele.

evidence.reference_title: Loss of function of SLC25A46 causes lethal congenital pontocerebellar hypoplasia.
evidence.snippet: In siblings from two unrelated families who died soon after birth with a profound neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by pontocerebellar hypoplasia and apnoea, we discovered a missense mutation and an exonic deletion in the SLC25A46 gene encoding a mitochondrial protein recently implicated in optic atrophy spectrum disorder.

evidence.reference_title: Loss of function of SLC25A46 causes lethal congenital pontocerebellar hypoplasia.
evidence.snippet: This genotype-phenotype correlation underscores the importance of SLC25A46 and fine tuning of mitochondrial fission and fusion in pontocerebellar hypoplasia and central neurodevelopment in addition to optic and peripheral neuropathy across the life span.

nodes.description: Mutations in RARS2, encoding the mitochondrial arginyl-tRNA synthetase, reduce aminoacylation of mitochondrial tRNA-Arg. This impairs mitochondrial translation, decreases oxidative phosphorylation capacity, and leads to energy failure preferentially in high-metabolic-demand cells of the developing cerebellum and pons. Elevated CSF lactate and reduced respiratory chain complex activity are biochemical hallmarks.

nodes.description: Biallelic mutations in the structural subunits of the nine-subunit RNA exosome impair RNA processing and turnover and cause the PCH1 subtypes: EXOSC3 gives PCH1B, EXOSC8 gives PCH1C, and EXOSC9 gives PCH1D. This mechanism produces pontocerebellar hypoplasia with spinal muscular atrophy-like weakness and global developmental delay, but survival and clinical severity vary by genotype. In zebrafish and human cell models, loss of exosome subunits stabilises p53 and perturbs ribosome biogenesis, which has been proposed as the route from exosome deficiency to the neuronal loss seen in PCH1.

nodes.description: Two PCH genes act on the maturation and function of small nuclear RNAs and the major spliceosome rather than on tRNA. TOE1 is a deadenylase that trims snRNA 3' ends, and PPIL1 is a peptidyl-prolyl isomerase component of the spliceosome. These are two steps in one pathway rather than two categories: the snRNAs TOE1 matures are components of the spliceosome PPIL1 belongs to, so biallelic loss of either gene converges on the same defect, loss of splicing integrity in developing neurons, giving PCH7 and PCH14 respectively.

nodes.description: The tRNA splicing endonuclease (TSEN) complex, composed of TSEN2, TSEN15, TSEN34, and TSEN54, cleaves introns from pre-tRNA molecules at the canonical anticodon loop position. Mutations in TSEN54 (and other TSEN subunits) impair pre-tRNA processing, reducing the pool of mature, functional tRNAs available for translation. Developing pontocerebellar neurons have exceptionally high translational demands and are disproportionately vulnerable. This mechanism maps primarily to PCH2/PCH4 for TSEN genes and to PCH10 for CLP1. The TSEN complex also interacts with CLP1, an RNA kinase, reinforcing RNA-processing as the central pathogenic pathway.
